title: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in-place (slow=insert position, fast=scan).
shortTitle: Remove Duplicates from a Sorted Array In-Place
keyPoints: Use two pointers: slow marks the last unique position, fast scans ahead for the next distinct value.
The precondition is that the array is already sorted, so duplicates are always adjacent.
When fast finds a new value, increment slow and copy the value there, compacting uniques to the front.
The unique count is slow + 1; elements beyond that are stale and should be ignored.
Java arrays cannot shrink, so the method returns the new logical length and the caller respects that prefix.
For BigDecimal, use compareTo for numeric equality to handle scale differences correctly.

s1_definition.oneliner: Slow pointer holds the last unique value; when fast finds a new value, bump slow and copy it there.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Two pointers** – `slow` marks the end of the unique prefix, `fast` scans for the next distinct value.
- **Sorted precondition** – duplicates are adjacent, so a single linear scan can collapse them.
- **Compact to front** – unique values are compacted into the front of the array.
- **Return new length** – the unique count is `slow + 1`; the caller ignores elements beyond that.
- **O(n) time, O(1) space** – one pass with no extra data structures.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has a sorted list of account identifiers from a settlement run, but the raw list repeats each identifier once per transaction. The bank wants each identifier only once. A clerk keeps a finger on the last unique identifier and scans ahead; every time the scanning finger lands on a new identifier, the clerk writes it just after the kept position.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses two pointers. A slow pointer marks the last unique position, and a fast pointer scans ahead. Because the array is sorted, duplicates are adjacent, so whenever fast finds a value different from slow, I increment slow and copy the new value there. The unique count is slow plus one, and it is all done in one linear pass with constant extra space.

The honest contract is that Java arrays cannot shrink, so the method compacts the distinct values into the front prefix and returns the new logical length. The caller must use only that prefix and ignore the stale tail.

For BigDecimal, I use compareTo to detect duplicates so that scale-different representations of the same account are correctly collapsed.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to collapse a sorted list of account identifiers from a settlement run so the notification service messages each distinct account exactly once.

Remember one sentence: slow marks the unique frontier, fast scans ahead, and a mismatch means advance slow and copy.
